fullText:
Final Steelers injury report ahead of Week 2 game vs. Patriots appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The Pittsburgh Steelers will travel to Foxborough without two starters after wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. and cornerback Joey Porter Jr. were ruled out for Sunday's Week 2 matchup. Pittman was downgraded Saturday, while Porter will miss his second straight game.

Pittman began the week as a limited participant because of a foot injury, then missed practice Thursday and Friday. Pittsburgh designated him questionable before ruling him out Saturday. Porter practiced on a limited basis all week while rebuilding his conditioning, but a back issue was added to his designation Thursday.

Left tackle Troy Fautanu remains questionable with an ankle injury. His progression offers optimism: Fautanu went from no practice Wednesday to limited work Thursday and full participation during Friday's walkthrough. Tight end Darnell Washington and defensive tackle Cameron Heyward practiced fully Friday and received no game designations.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The #Steelers have downgraded WR Michael Pittman Jr. to OUT for Sunday's game with a foot injury.

— Burt Lauten (@SteelersPRBurt) September 19, 2026

Pittman's injury removes the leading receiver in Pittsburgh's season-opening 20-13 victory over Atlanta. The veteran caught all three of his targets for a team-high 58 yards, with two 20-yard gains. He also played 59 offensive snaps, or 88% of Pittsburgh's total.

Without him, DK Metcalf becomes the centerpiece of the passing game. Metcalf drew 10 targets in Week 1 but converted them into only four receptions for 40 yards. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers will likely target him aggressively, particularly in key situations, but Pittsburgh needs more efficiency from that connection.

Roman Wilson and rookie Germie Bernard should receive more playing time. Wilson already played 37 snaps in the opener, while Bernard appeared on only three offensive plays. The second-round rookie caught five passes for 64 yards and a touchdown, and can now join the rotation.

Pittsburgh could also compensate with heavier tight-end personnel. Washington's return from a personal absence gives the Steelers their blocking specialist, while Pat Freiermuth offers Rodgers a dependable target. Freiermuth caught five passes for 46 yards and Pittsburgh's only offensive touchdown in Week 1.

Porter's continued absence places Asante Samuel Jr. in line to start again. Porter spent training camp on the physically unable to perform list because of his back and is rebuilding his conditioning. He left Thursday's practice with a trainer before the back designation reappeared, preventing his return.

The Steelers must now lean on Samuel and Jamel Dean as their primary outside cornerbacks, with rookie Daylen Everette positioned as the next option. That arrangement held up during the opening victory, but Porter's press-man ability and physical coverage style cannot be replicated. Pittsburgh may mix zone and man coverages while providing more safety assistance outside.

Fautanu's status is the remaining major question. A full Friday workload is highly encouraging and suggests he has a realistic chance to start and play every snap. If he cannot play, Pittsburgh would likely move Dylan Cook to left tackle and insert first-round rookie Max Iheanachor on the right side, disrupting both tackle spots.

The final report is relatively short, but the two confirmed absences remove important players from opposite sides of the ball. Pittsburgh must replace Pittman's route volume and production while again operating without its top cover cornerback. Metcalf, Wilson, Bernard and Freiermuth must collectively fill the offensive void, while Samuel and Dean carry increased responsibility defensively.

A 1-0 start gives the Steelers valuable early-season momentum, but Sunday will truly measure their overall depth. Winning on the road will require Rodgers to distribute the ball very effectively, the offensive line to remain stable and Pittsburgh's replacement cornerbacks to avoid surrendering explosive plays.

title: Rienk Mast one of four players signed to Exhibit 10 deals with Pacers
description: Rink Mast, Keiba Keta, Kowalcie Reeves and Jalen Warley signed Exhibit 10 deals with the Pacers
fullText:
Former Nebraska center Rienk Mast -- one of the Pacers' top performers at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas in July -- was one of four players signed to Exhibit 10 contracts by the Pacers on Saturday.

The Pacers also signed former BYU center Keiba Keta, former Georgia Tech forward Kowacie Reeves Jr. and former Gonzaga wing Jalen Warley to Exhibit 10 deals. They also signed forwards Keion Brooks Jr., and M.J. Iraldi and guards Wade Taylor IV and Cam Hildreth to Exhibit 10 deals earlier this week.

Exhibit 10 contracts are formally considered one-year, non-guaranteed minimum salary contracts, but their more pertinent function is to provide a bonus for players to stay in the G League. Players who sign Exhibit 10 deals who are then waived by the parent club can make a bonus of up to $91,000 if they spend at least 60 days on the roster of that team's G League affiliate in the 2026-27 season. Brooks, Iraldi, Taylor and Hildreth have already been waived and Mast, Keta, Reeves, and Warley will likely also be waived shortly and end up on the roster of the Noblesville Boom.

Mast finished second on the Pacers' Summer League roster in scoring and first in rebounding in July, averaging 15.3 points and 9.0 rebounds per game and shooting 47.9% from the floor including 33.3% from 3-point range. Forward Jalen Slawson (20.8 ppg) was the only player who averaged more points and he will start the season on a two-way contract. Mast, a 6-10, 250-pound, 25-year-old native of the Netherlands, spent seven seasons in college due to injury and the COVID pandemic and averaged 13.3 points and 5.8 rebounds last season for Nebraska.

title: Gophers take care of business, beating Akron 41-7
description: It was a gloomy day in the Twin Cities and a lethargic crowd supported a Gopher team that moved to 2-1 as they head into Big Ten play. After a deflating loss to Mississippi State last week, the Gophers came out and did exactly what they were supposed to do, beating the Akron Zips 41-7. […]
fullText:
It was a gloomy day in the Twin Cities and a lethargic crowd supported a Gopher team that moved to 2-1 as they head into Big Ten play. After a deflating loss to Mississippi State last week, the Gophers came out and did exactly what they were supposed to do, beating the Akron Zips 41-7. The Gophers were better in all three phases and secured their first shutout against an FBS opponent since beating Nevada 27-0 in 2024.

Akron lost their starting quarterback, Cibastian Broughton, to a knee injury in the first quarter and the Zips offense struggled to pose any threat to the Gopher defense throughout all four quarters.

Minnesota took control early and never relinquished. Freshman Quayd Hendryx took the opening kickoff and returned it 42 yards, giving the offense a short field to start the game. Drake Lindsey then hit Noah Jennings for 30 yards on first down and four plays later, Lindsey hit Roman Voss for his first career touchdown.

Akron's response to that opening touchdown was a four-play drive before Joey Gerlach forced a fumble that was recovered by TJ Bush Jr.

From that point on, it wasn't as if Minnesota thoroughly dominated the game, but the outcome was never in doubt. Their next four possessions were a punt (following the fumble recovery), an interception, a field goal and then another punt. But the Gopher defense kept the Zips in check, forcing four punts and a fourth-down stop to keep Akron at zero.

The offense, on Lindsey's arm, scored 10 more points in the second quarter. Jennings made a fantastic catch to score from six yards out. And Drzewiecki hit a 43-yard field goal to give Minnesota 20-0 lead at the half.

The third quarter was much of the same. Akron punted on all three of their possessions and Minnesota continued to move the ball through the air, with very little ground game.

Near the end of the third quarter, the Gopher offense had run 43 plays. 31 of those were pass attempts and just 12 rushing attempts, with three of those being Drake Lindsey. They had 12 rushing attempts for a total of 13 yards, after completely abandoning the run in the second half last week. The lack of being able to run the ball was beginning to become a huge concern.

Then, the strangest thing happened. Minnesota started running the ball and they ran it effectively. With 4:46 remaining in the third quarter, the Gopher offense started running the ball and they didn't pass the rest of the game. It started on first down with a TJ Thomas rush for eight yards; the longest rush since the Eastern Illinois game. That was followed by five more rushing attempts that resulted in two first downs.

Thomas took the ball on the first play of the fourth quarter and ran for 20 yards. AJ Turner was given the ball on the following play and he ran for 17. Three plays later, all rushes, Turner ran into the end zone from the four, pushing the score to 34-0.

Akron had a quick three-and-out, and Minnesota took the ball on their own 29. Thomas took the drive's initial handoff and went nearly untouched for a 71-yard touchdown. At that point, it was 12 consecutive rushing attempts for 142 yards. The team had 160 yards rushing combined in their first two games.

With the score 41-0, the second string came into the game. Akron managed to put together one scoring drive and the game ended 41-7.

The game was never in doubt, but Minnesota showing they could effectively run the ball was an encouraging end to an otherwise vanilla game.

Up next, Minnesota travels to Washington to open Big Ten play next week. It is a 10:00 PM kickoff, so get your rest on Friday.

title: Tee times moved up for Biltmore Championship final round due to thunderstorms
description: Tee times for the final round of the Biltmore Championship in Asheville on Sept. 20 have been moved up to avoid thunderstorms in the afternoon.
fullText:
The PGA Tour is moving up tee times for the final round of the Biltmore Championship Asheville as the threat of thunderstorms linger over western North Carolina.

The first tee times for the final round on Sept. 20 will be between 7:43 a.m. ET and 9:55 am ET, the PGA Tour announced in a news release on Sept. 19. Parking lot shuttles for spectators will begin to run at 6:15 a.m. and entry gates to the Cliffs at Walnut Cover will open at 7 a.m.

The current forecast calls for a 40% chance of thunderstorms in Asheville beginning at 2 p.m. ET on Sept. 20. The chance of thunderstorms increases to 60% by 4 p.m. ET.

"Fans should be aware that conditions on the property may be wet," The PGA Tour said. "All fans should dress accordingly and use caution in areas where water has accumulated, as well as mounding and hills, which might be slippery."

Real time updates will be provided via the Biltmore Championship's social media accounts on X, Instagram and Facebook.

Weather has now adjusted schedules for three of four days at the Biltmore Championship Asheville. The first round started a half an hour later than originally scheduled due to fog and the start of second round play was move dup by an hour to avoid thunderstorms in the afternoon.

fullText:
19 September 1926 to 19 September 2026. One hundred years of San Siro, one hundred years of history that have impacted both the city of Milano and world football. Inaugurated by a 6-3 derby win for Inter, San Siro (known as the Stadio Giuseppe Meazza) has, with the passing of time, become a timeless symbol.

From the intuition of Piero Pirello to the continued growth of the ground, from the World Cups in '24 and '90 to its most iconic European nights, as well as big concerts and international events, San Siro has played host to a wealth of emotions that go beyond football and has borne witness to some of the greatest moments in Inter's history.

To celebrate San Siro's centenary, on Inter.it, we have published an interactive special for you to relive these 100 years. The images, facts, and stories include newspaper pieces, tales of Inter's biggest wins, and the people, events, and moments that have made the Meazza legendary.

A journey through a century-long history. A journey inside San Siro.

title: Saturday afternoon Orioles game thread: vs. Brewers, 4:05
description: Where the Birds keep coming close to mathematical elimination from the playoffs, and Félix Bautista is reinstated.
fullText:
Look, it's not like the reasonable among us expected to win every game against the Brewers, current owners of the MLB's best record. But last night was frankly a bummer. The Orioles had loads of baserunners and yet—that old saw—couldn't drive them in. The Baltimore Sun reports today that GM Mike Elias and manager Craig Albernaz expect to be back to with the team next season. Fine, but I hope the approach to hitting with runners on base gets a major overhaul—it needs to.

Baltimore belatedly announced that today's starter (stopper) would be Trevor Rogers (10-10, 4.22, 143 SO in 157.2 IP). The lefty last pitched on Sept. 13, six days ago, a blah outing against the Blue Jays where he allowed four runs in six innings in a loss. But before that, he had two strong starts against Cleveland and Colorado. Rogers' pre-All Star Break ERA is 4.48; post it's 3.88.

In pitching news from the back end of the bullpen, the Orioles just reinstated closer Félix Bautista, who hasn't appeared in a game in over a year. It's too late in the season to make much of a difference, but man, it'll be good to see The Mountain trotting out to the mound in late innings instead of guys like Alex Hoppe or Andrew Kittredge. The O's skipper hasn't committed to using Bautista as a closer yet, so perhaps expect in him a bridge role.

Starting for the Brewers today is Robert Gasser, initially one of four arms the Brewers acquired in 2022 via the trade for closer Josh Hader. Now in his third season with Milwaukee, it's a little soon to assess Gasser's value, as he missed long stretches due to Tommy John surgery. This season, he started out with Milwaukee's Triple-A team and since joining the team in late May, has been pretty much average, with a 4.30 ERA in 18 starts.

As our own Mark pointed out in the series preview, Gasser's Statcast peripherals fail to inspire confidence. Gasser has a five-pitch mix, but his sweeper, his most-thrown pitch, has a -6 run value, his worst of any. His fastball is also below-average, per Statcast. He doesn't throw the ball hard, he doesn't get a lot of whiffs, and he doesn't get batters to chase outside of the strike zone very often.

Gasser is left-handed, so the Orioles have stuffed their lineup with righties… not that you will necessarily love all the names. Jeremiah Jackson makes a rare appearance in the leadoff spot, and the bottom four hitters include three righties in Rece Hinds, Christian Franklin, and Leody Taveras (switch-hitter). Well. At least Alonso and Mayo, in the second and third spots, are hot right now.

title: MLB insider reveals Yankees have 'no idea' if Aaron Judge will play again in 2026
description: This is a very concerning update for the Yankees and Aaron Judge.
fullText:
MLB insider reveals Yankees have 'no idea' if Aaron Judge will play again in 2026 originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The New York Yankees have played the majority of the 2026 MLB season without Aaron Judge. He landed on the injured list right after the end of May, although he did return for a brief period of time.

Unfortunately, Judge tweaked his calf and hit the injured list for a second time this season. Unlike his earlier stint, this one might end his season.

According to MLB insider Bob Nightengale of USA Today, Judge's injury has left the Yankees with "no idea" if he'll play again this season. Judge, a key to the Yankees' success this postseason, might be out for the rest of the year.

"The New York Yankees, who have played without All-Star outfielder Aaron Judge for most of the season, are bracing themselves now for the possibility that their three-time MVP may not play again the rest of the season," Nightengale writes. "... The Yankees have no idea whether he can play again this season."

Judge was out for a long time due to a rib issue, but returned in August with the hopes of being a contributor down the stretch. He didn't go through a rehab assignment and tried helping out at the big-league level right away.

Now, he's back on the IL due to a right calf strain and will miss 10 days at minimum, which would bring him to the end of the regular season.

MORE: Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski makes all kinds of MLB history with 1,000 pitches of 100 mph

He might come back in time for the playoffs, but there would likely be a lot of concern about his production if he does come back, as the questions about his health will be very real.

Aaron Boone told reporters recently, "I don't know," regarding whether Judge would play again or not. That's not the kind of update Yankees fans will like to hear.

Unfortunately, with the postseason just a few weeks away, Yankees fans should expect to be without Judge for quite a while, if not for the rest of the 2026 season, including the playoffs.

The Yankees, entering play on Saturday, September 19, are 89-64 and have clinched a postseason spot already. As they try to make up ground in the AL East race and begin the MLB playoffs, they're likely to do so with Judge, as his return is unknown.

fullText:
After a record setting night in Devaney on Friday, the Huskers will look to close out the Ameritas Players Challenge with a 2-0 record and, hopefully, their 1st sweep of the weekend. The Huskers hosted #25 North Carolina on Friday night and what looked like what as going to be a sweep, turned into a 4 set match with the Tar Heels.

Even though the 2nd set looked rough, they still managed to set a record: most service aces in the Devaney Center with 13 of them. Their serving has come a long way since the senior classes freshman year when we had to have had at least 10 service errors a match.

North Carolina and FGCU will play today and the Huskers will have the day off to rest and recharge before the finale match on Sunday.

Florida Gulf Coast Eagles
2025 Record: 19-9
2025 Conference Record: 13-3 (ASUN Conference)
Last NCAA Tournament Appearance: 2024 (Lost to Marquette in First Round)

FGCU have had a winning standard in their program for years and years. They have had winning seasons dating all the way back to 2013 being their last losing season with a 14-19 record.

They started the 2026 season kind of slow though with a 3-5 record. All 3 losses came to Power teams losing to #24 BYU, Florida State, and West Virginia. Nebraska expects to continue this trend for them on Sunday afternoon.g

They won the ASUN Regular Season in 2025, their 9th regular-season crown, but not the Tournament. Their last tournament win doesn't date that far back though as they won their conference tournament in 2o24 beating Queens, Eastern Kentucky, and Lipscomb to clinch it. They had won 4 consecutive ASUN titles before losing in 2025 to North Florida in the Quarterfinals.

That win also clinched them a NCAA tournament appearance as well. They have consistently been making the tournament qualifying in 2018 and then 2021-2024. Their best finish in the NCAA tournament was both in 2018 and 2021 when they made it to the 2nd Round. They ultimately lost to Florida in 2018 and Wisconsin in 2021.

FGCU is the favorite again this year to win the ASUN, receiving all but 2 first-place votes in the preseason coaches poll. #2 Jacksonville and #5 Queens received the other votes.

The Eagles offense is led by both a senior and a freshman this year with both making some noise on the team right out of the gates. They both played all sets this season and make up for 48% of the teams kills so far.

Senior OH Julija Grubisic Cabo is part of the ASUN Preseason Team this year and her stats are already showing us why she is. She has 94 kills and is averaging 3.03 kills/set. She is also 2nd on the team in digs with 77, just behind the libero Anna Marzella.

Freshman OPP Maju Hildebrand has been making herself known early in this season with the team high 99 kills, averaging 3.19 a set. Hildebrand is from Brazil and was named the MVP of all Brazilian Clubs and the Best Opposite of all Brazilian Clubs last year. She also represented the Brazilian National Team in 2024.

The Eagles could run a 6-2 at some point with both Seniors Eliska Vytiskova and Dinara Sabitova getting almost equal playing time this season. Sabitova has been their go-to though playing every set and averaging 6.81 assists/set.

Even though FGCU is a powerhouse in their conference, they are about to run into one of the top powerhouse programs in the country on Sunday afternoon. Sunday's match will begin at 12:00pm CST and will be available to stream on B1G+.

title: Hansi Flick explains choosing Livaković over Szczęsny for Barcelona vs Sevilla
description: Barcelona head coach Hansi Flick has provided an explanation for his decision to field Dominik Livaković over Wojciech Szczęsny from the off in the club’s latest outing.Barcelona are of course cur...
fullText:
Barcelona head coach Hansi Flick has provided an explanation for his decision to field Dominik Livaković over Wojciech Szczęsny from the off in the club's latest outing.

Barcelona are of course currently locked in action on the domestic front. Eyeing a seventh win from seven to open the defence of their La Liga title, the Blaugrana have made the trip to The Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán, to lock horns with Sevilla.

The visitors headed into proceedings sans the services of star goalkeeper Joan García, ruled out owing to an injury suffered against Racing Santander in midweek.

After Wojciech Szczęsny was introduced off the bench versus Racing, the widespread expectation was that the experienced Pole would be in from the off in Sevilla on Saturday.

Upon Barcelona's starting line-up being announced, however, it was summer signing Dominik Livaković who featured between the posts.

Speaking to the media ahead of kick-off, Hansi Flick was therefore drawn on his goalkeeper call for the evening. And the German tactician went on to explain:

"Livaković over Szczesny? We analysed everything, and we decided that we needed a change in the goalkeeper position. And that's what we did."

title: Mizzou Volleyball Outlasts Bowling Green in Four-Set Thriller
description: Led by breakout performance off from Stahley, the Tigers closed out trip to Ohio on a high note.
fullText:
Coming off a frustrating pair of five-set losses the day prior, Missouri volleyball desperately needed a bounce-back win. With a rescheduled date against No. 1 Nebraska looming ahead, Dawn Sullivan's squad showed up and showed out, holding off the Falcons in four sets (25-16, 24-26, 25-20, 25-23).

Led by freshmen Lydia Stahley (11 kills) and Eva Smith (nine kills), Mizzou generated clutch late-set scoring runs to seal the match. The victory marked the Tigers' sole win of the Bowling Green/Toledo Invitational.

For the first time all weekend, Mizzou set the tone early by jumping out to a quick opening-set victory.

Paige Felder got the offense rolling, followed by early kills from Grace O'Reilly and Kimani Johnson to stake Mizzou to a 5-1 lead. Bowling Green struggled with consistency behind the service line, giving away points that allowed the Tigers to stay comfortably ahead.

Midway through the set, Sierra Dudley put on a serving showcase, dropping multiple aces alongside kills from Lauren Larkin and Maizy Agnello to blow the frame open at 14-6. Ainoah Cruz anchored the back row with sharp court coverage, allowing Smith and Larkin to assert themselves at the net down the stretch. Agnello capped off a dominant set with a crisp service ace to claim frame one.

Bowling Green brought vastly improved net discipline into set two, capitalizing on early Mizzou attack errors to jump out to a 10-4 advantage.

Looking for a spark, Sullivan brought Lydia Stahley into the rotation, a move that immediately paid off. Stahley quickly came in with a kill, starting a rally that featured swings from Johnson to bring Mizzou back within strike distance at 15-11.

Trailing 20-16 late, the Tigers mounted a tough comeback. Key attack errors from the Falcons, paired with consecutive kills from Stahley, leveled the frame at 22-22. Mizzou even earned set point at 24-22 following another Falcon error, but Bowling Green refused to go down. The Falcons strung together four consecutive points, closing on back-to-back kills to shock the Tigers and snatch set two.

Rather than letting the late set-two collapse their momentum, Mizzou responded early on. Kills from O'Reilly and Smith, paired with a Piper Batie service ace, powered Mizzou to an early 6-3 advantage.

Bowling Green briefly threatened to close the gap midway through the frame, but Stahley completely took over the match from the service line. The freshman attacker went on a scorching run, firing off three consecutive service aces to turn a tight 19-15 contest into a commanding 22-15 lead.

The Falcons managed to save four set points late in the frame during a brief Mizzou lapse, although a Falcons service error finally sealed the victory for the Tigers, putting Mizzou back on top 2-1.

Set four proved to be a back-to-back battle, featuring 12 ties and multiple lead changes as both teams traded heavy blows.

Mizzou relied heavily on their front-row blocking, getting early rejections from Smith and sophomore Maca Lobaglio to stay neck-and-neck. The Falcons used aggressive serving to push ahead 18-15, but Stahley once again delivered in the clutch, pounding back-to-back kills to tie the score at 18-18.

With the set locked at 20-20, Mizzou made the critical final push. Smith terminated a clutch swing to put Mizzou up 22-20, while junior middle blocker Tia Phinezy stepped back to serve and delivered a massive service ace for a 23-20 lead.

The Falcons refused to quit, clawing back to tie the game at 23-23 off a Mizzou attack error. With the match on the line, Paige Felder stepped up with a monster roll shot kill to set up match point at 24-23. On the next rally, pressure at the net forced a final Falcon attack error, locking up the Tigers victory.

Stahley finished with a .409 hitting %, four service aces and a 15.0 total point performance off the bench. Smith had a stellar.438 hitting %, six total blocks, one service ace and 13.5 points. Ainoah Cruz claimed 22 digs, five assists and dominant back-row defense. Piper Batie & Sierra Dudley combined for 31 assists to orchestrate the offense.

With a vital win secured to avoid a winless weekend, the Tigers will immediately pivot to their toughest test of the season. A rescheduled road clash against top-ranked No. 1 Nebraska in Lincoln will set the tone Wednesday, at 6 p.m.

title: ZK-JPEG: Zero-Knowledge Image Editing and Compression
description: Tools for generating deep fake photographs are proliferating with greater ease of use and prominence in pop culture. Image authentication tools can defeat these deceitful developments by verifying that a digital image was actually produced by a physical camera. The challenge is that these tools must be robust to desirable image transformations.
fullText:
Paper 2026/2039
 ZK-JPEG: Zero-knowledge Image Editing and Compression

 Samuel Dittmer, Stealth Software Technologies, Inc.

 Steve Lu, Stealth Software Technologies, Inc.

 Kimberlee Model, Stealth Software Technologies, Inc.

 Joseph Near, University of Vermont

 Abstract
 Tools for generating deep fake photographs are proliferating with greater ease of use and prominence in pop culture. Image authentication tools can defeat these deceitful developments by verifying that a digital image was actually produced by a physical camera. The challenge is that these tools must be robust to desirable image transformations.
Camera attestation uses digital signatures to prove an image's provenance from a camera. Lossy compression makes minute changes in order to reduce an image's size, and blurring or redacting regions of an image can protect its subjects. These changes invalidate an image's signature. Prior works use zero-knowledge (ZK) to prove a published image's edit history, but they do not survive lossy encoding such as the JPEG format.
We present \zkjpeg, a cryptographic tool for JPEG compression that proves an image was correctly compressed from a secret, committed input. In addition, our tool can verify a large family of image transformations by integrating them into JPEG compression with minimal cost.
Our system is fast, flexible, and can be instantiated from off-the-shelf ZK tools. We use PicoZK to convert Python image editing code into a ZK circuit for the line-point zero knowledge (LPZK) proof system.

title: Jevmetrics – probabilistic metric reduction inside OpenTelemetry
description: Contribute to ishantanu/jevmetrics development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
Jev inference for metric assessment and retention in OpenTelemetry.

jevmetrics is an experimental metrics-to-metrics OpenTelemetry Collector connector. It calls TypeSafe’s Jev model to infer the likely operational value of metric instruments from their metadata, then applies deterministic policy to the returned probabilities.

Use it to assess unfamiliar instrumentation, review candidates for reduced retention, and selectively filter metrics before they reach a primary backend. Inference runs asynchronously, and cached assessments let subsequent batches use the same decision without another API call.

Status: alpha. Start with annotate, which preserves incoming metrics and exports the assessments for review. Filtering effectiveness and cost savings need evaluation on your own telemetry.

A new service or library can introduce metrics nobody has classified yet. Names, descriptions, units, instrumentation scope, and attribute keys provide evidence about what those metrics mean—even before there is a history of dashboard or query usage.

jevmetrics uses that evidence to ask Jev whether a metric is likely useful enough to retain. Explicit protection rules and thresholds determine what the Collector actually does with the answer.

The defining feature is model inference as a runtime step in telemetry retention policy. The connector constructs typed questions, sends them to Jev, validates the answers, and turns one of those probabilities into a keep/drop decision.

This complements existing approaches:

The project explores a specific combination: semantic metric assessment through Jev, execution within an OTel Collector connector, and retention decisions before export to a chosen backend.

For an unprotected metric without a fresh cached assessment, the connector:

Each request contains four questions:

A noul expresses the probability of a yes/no judgment. The recommended action and the other probabilities are exposed for review; they do not override the keep-score policy. See the TypeSafe API reference for the primitive definitions.

Inference happens remotely in Jev. The Collector handles metadata extraction, scheduling, caching, and policy execution locally. No model training takes place in the connector.

The example receives OTLP/gRPC on port 4317 and OTLP/HTTP on port 4318, and sends annotated metrics to the debug exporter. It also has independent logs and traces pipelines; the connector only processes metrics.

In another terminal, send a sample metric:

The original metric should appear in the Collector output. After successful inference, look for the Jev metric score received log and the four jev.metric.* companion metrics below. The batch processor may delay debug output. Scores are model judgments, so the quickstart does not prescribe numeric results.

If only the original metric appears, check for scoring errors, a valid API key, and access to the configured endpoint. A successful OTLP request confirms ingestion, not successful inference.

Keep both _build/otelcol-jevmetrics and _build/otelcol-jevmetrics-core together when moving the build. The launcher delegates Collector commands to the adjacent core binary. VERSION supplies the launcher version; components lists the compiled components.

route and reduce execute the same filtering logic. The archive fan-out is part of the Collector pipeline configuration; the connector does not create it automatically.

Filtering removes an entire metric and its datapoints for the assessed identity. There is no downsampling, dimension reduction, or automatic aggregation. A Jev recommendation of reduce is advisory and does not implement those operations.

In annotate, successful inference emits these gauges immediately through the downstream pipeline and includes them again with subsequent batches that use a cached score:

Companion datapoints carry metric.name and jev.model, under the original resource and instrumentation scope. Original datapoints are not modified. Annotation adds telemetry volume. Protected metrics bypass inference and do not receive companion assessments.

For a local Prometheus endpoint on port 9464, use config-local.yaml.

The connector appears as an exporter in the input metrics pipeline and as a receiver in the output metrics pipeline. Complete working configurations are in examples/otelcol.

All shown values are defaults except api_key, which is required, and protected_metrics, which is empty by default. The protected metric above is an example; explicitly list the metrics needed by your alerts and SLOs.

In route and reduce, the default thresholds mean:

Thresholds must be in [0, 1], with drop_threshold <= keep_threshold. If both thresholds are equal, a score at that boundary is kept. annotate preserves input regardless of scores.

Unscored metrics are retained. This includes first-seen metrics, expired or evicted assessments, a full scoring queue, and unsuccessful inference attempts. Invalid answer types, missing probabilities, out-of-range probabilities, and unsupported actions are treated as failures.

After a scoring failure, the connector pauses new inference requests for one second, doubling after successive failures up to 32 seconds. Already-running requests may complete; a successful response resets the cooldown. Future incoming batches trigger retries after the cooldown.

Fresh cached decisions remain effective during an API outage, including decisions to drop metrics. When those scores expire, the metrics are kept until a fresh assessment arrives. Fail-open behavior concerns the inference path; it does not guarantee delivery through an unavailable downstream exporter.

The in-memory cache uses least-recently-used eviction at capacity. Expired scores are removed on lookup and during periodic cleanup. Cache identity includes the complete resource attributes, instrumentation scope name/version/attributes, schema URLs, and instrument name, description, unit, type, temporality, and monotonicity where applicable. Restarting the Collector clears its assessments.

Queue and cache limits bound entry counts, not metadata bytes or input batch size. Attribute keys and observed series counts are refreshed when rescoring occurs; changing those alone does not invalidate a fresh cached assessment.

Raw metric values, histogram buckets, exemplars, and datapoint attribute values are not included in the inference request. Datapoint attribute values are examined locally to estimate distinct series. Metric metadata and allowed resource values can still contain sensitive information; choose the allow-list accordingly.

The original resource is preserved in exported telemetry and companion metrics. The allow-list controls what goes to Jev, not what goes to your telemetry backend.

Gauge, Sum, Histogram, Exponential Histogram, and Summary are supported. Retained metrics keep their original payloads. See SEMCONV.md for data-model details.

Jev evaluates one metric summary at a time. It does not receive historical values, other metric inventories, query history, dashboard dependencies, alert rules, or SLO definitions. Redundancy is therefore a semantic estimate, not a measured correlation with another signal. A keep probability is not evidence that dropping a metric is operationally safe.

The project does not yet provide:

Evaluate in annotate first: compare assessments with engineer-reviewed decisions, protect critical metrics, and measure inference overhead and added telemetry. Before enabling filtering, verify the prospective savings and missed-signal rate on representative workloads. An archive branch can preserve the full stream while you evaluate the filtered primary stream.

The connector is implemented in otelconnector. The OCB manifest includes OTLP reception/export, debug and Prometheus exporters, memory limiting, batching, and the connector. It uses a local module replacement for development.

Tests cover response validation, mode normalization, retention policy, payload preservation across metric types, queue saturation, cache identity/expiry/eviction, and failure recovery. They use a mock HTTP transport; live Jev inference and production assessment quality require separate validation. See BUILD_NOTES.md for recorded verification.

This repository also contains an earlier standalone Prometheus polling experiment in cmd/jevmetrics. It assesses service anomalies and impact using a separate evaluator. The root Dockerfile, make build, and make run target that application; they do not build or run the OTel connector. The Collector path described above is the primary project direction.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for development checks and pull request
guidance, and SECURITY.md for vulnerability reporting.

GitHub Actions runs formatting, vet, and race tests for
both modules, then builds the Collector and validates all example configurations.
CI uses mock inference responses and a placeholder key; no Jev credentials are
required. Run make check locally and make collector-validate after a Collector
build. Dependabot checks GitHub Actions and connector dependencies weekly.

title: Solving rubiks cubes "without search"
description: In classical AI, perception relies on learning state-based representations, while planning, which can be thought of as temporal reasoning over action sequences, is typically achieved through search. We study whether such reasoning can instead emerge from representations that capture both perceptual and temporal structure. We show that standard temporal contrastive learning, despite its popularity, often fails to capture temporal structure due to its reliance on spurious features. To address this, we introduce Combinatorial Representations for Temporal Reasoning (CRTR), a method that uses a negative sampling scheme to provably remove these spurious features and facilitate temporal reasoning. CRTR achieves strong results on domains with complex temporal structure, such as Sokoban and Rubik's Cube.

title: Escaping Docker's Hypervisor
description: We reported a sandbox escape in Docker's hypervisor for Mac: a container gets complete read and write access to the host filesystem with three lines of bash. Assigned CVE-2026-77179 and fixed in Docker Desktop 4.88.0 and Docker Sandboxes 0.42.
fullText:
Docker has patched a sandbox escape we reported in its hypervisor for Mac: a container can get complete read and write access to the host filesystem by running three lines of bash.

Docker Desktop and Docker Sandboxes are both affected. Docker Desktop is only affected if Docker VMM is turned on in Settings. It’s a good thing we found it now, because Docker VMM is scheduled to become the default for Docker Desktop at the end of October 2026.

The vulnerability has been assigned CVE-2026-77179, and has been fixed in Docker Sandboxes 0.42.0 and Docker Desktop 4.88.0.

When you mount a folder into a container, Docker’s VMM uses virtio-fs, and the file server that serves it runs on the host. The first time the guest touches a path it sends a lookup, and the server answers with a nodeid: a number the server picked, for its own bookkeeping. From then on the guest asks by nodeid and never sends the path again, so the server has to find that file again on every request.

It has two ways to find it. First by inode, through macOS volfs. If that fails, it falls back to the path string it saved when the file was first looked up.

Deleting the file removes the volfs path. Holding it open keeps the nodeid. Together they leave the server with nothing but the string. Then the guest replaces the parent folder with a symlink. The server reads that string and sees a path that’s inside the mounted folder and allows it, but then the kernel reads the same string, follows the symlink, and opens a file on the host outside of the mounted folder.

The guest picks a file on the host that it wants to read or overwrite. Say /Users/you/.zshenv.

The server resolves that string one more time. pv is a symlink now, and it is not the last name in the path, so the kernel follows it. The request lands on /Users/you/.zshenv.

Sailor is the internal name of Docker’s hypervisor.

Docker’s security team was quick and professional. They replied in about seven hours and confirmed the bug in two days. The Docker Desktop fix shipped on August 24, and the Docker Sandboxes fix shipped in 0.42.0 on September 7.

If you use Docker Sandboxes, run sbx --version. Make sure you’re running 0.42.0 or later.

If you use Docker Desktop, you want 4.88.0 or later. Open Settings, General, Virtual Machine Manager. Any earlier version with Docker VMM selected is affected.

Agents run untrusted code all day, and the sandbox around them is the only thing between that code and the machine it runs on.

That sandbox is what we build at Accomplish: one environment for any agent, any model, any cloud.

title: Divide by Depth for Instant 3D
description: When I first started working on games, I used high level frameworks that would give you a Camera that just kind of worked. But as I learned more and wanted t...
fullText:
When I first started working on games, I used high level frameworks that would give you a Camera that just kind of worked. But as I learned more and wanted to apply more creative techniques, I struggled to even have the vocabulary to search for what I wanted to do, and only after writing lower level graphics code did I understand cameras are based around kind of really simple math.

In the excellent One Formula That Demystifies 3D Graphics (via @tsoding), we’re presented with the following:

In essence, if we say \(y\) is up and \(z\) is forward, 3D coordinates \((x, y, z)\) can be projected into 2D coordinates \((x', y')\) by dividing \(x\) and \(y\) by \(z\). For example, if we have a series of 3D points that only vary in depth, as depth increases, their projected positions get closer to vanishing point \((0,0)\):

This can be demonstrated by a ball that moves and scales with depth as it orbits the camera’s up axis, offset along the \(z\) axis by forward:

Using the same principle, we can even draw more sophisticated “geometry” in the same way!

Obviously, these are very constrained and naive examples that are largely impractical in all but the simplest scenarios. When we do any kind of 3D work, we typically need to involve things like the direction the camera’s pointing in, it’s position, it’s field of view, etc. While we could in theory hack those shaders to support these features, there is a way that’s less effort and more practical. It’s called the perspective projection matrix, and it’s the magic behind the mighty Camera.

There are a few ways to construct a perspective projection matrix, depending on your use case. Computer vision and graphics for example, have slightly different conventions for layout, which is why it’s hard to point to a single Wikipedia article and expect a universal form. That being said, in triangle-based graphics, a common convention that’s often followed involves parameterization of field of view, aspect ratio, and near and far clipping planes. These values are all very important because they also double as a way to easily know what’s in frame and what isn’t, which lets us render our scenes in performant ways, such as through culling off-screen geometry and rendering only what’s visible.

While this varies across different coordinate conventions (little consensus around which axes correspond to up, right, and forward), the general structure is mostly consistent:

This describes a camera with focal scale \(f\) (derived from vertical fov angle \(\theta\)) and aspect ratio \(a\):

Where \(A\) and \(B\) represent depth mapping, derived from near and far clipping planes \(n\) and \(F\) respectively:

So how does this connect to the depth division trick from earlier? Turns out that’s a special form of the perspective projection matrix.

Given a point somewhere in 3D space, we first describe its position relative to the camera. This takes us from world space, where coordinates are shared by the whole scene, into view space, where the camera sits at the origin. We then multiply by the perspective projection matrix, producing clip-space coordinates that are ready for the perspective division.

After dividing the first three clip-space components by \(w\), the coordinates no longer describe distances in the scene. Instead, they describe where the point falls inside the camera’s visible bounds. These are normalized device coordinates, usually shortened to NDC, which later allow points to finally be mapped to the screen’s output resolution.

In the earlier example, both focal scale \(f\) and aspect ratio \(a\) are omitted. Substituting them both with 1 gives us exactly the original depth division trick:

While the depth division trick works for camera-relative points in simple scenarios, it’s really just one step in the full graphics pipeline. Now that all of those terms have names, the whole journey looks like this:

If there’s one thing to take away from this writeup, it’s that Cameras are just doing a few simple transformations, and if you understand what each of those transformations are for, you can pick and choose which parts to implement yourself based off your own needs and constraints. Sometimes you need the entire pipeline, and sometimes you need that one depth division.

title: The End of Upward Mobility
description: Artificial intelligence is coming for the meritocracy.
fullText:
In April 1941, with the Wehrmacht in Paris and the Ribbentrop–Molotov pact still in force, the political theorist James Burnham published “The Managerial Revolution,” which famously declared that capitalism was finished. His claim was not that it ought to be finished, but that it was, as a matter of observable fact, being replaced. The successor system would not, however, be socialism, as he had hoped during his earlier days as a Trotskyist. Socialism, he argued, was a utopia: it required abundance, and since human wants are unlimited, abundance is unreachable.

What was coming instead was a new economic system he termed “managerialism,” in which the instruments of production pass to the state and the state passes them on to the men who know how to run things — managers. If capitalists survived at all, it would be merely as a decorative residue: playing golf in Florida while the managers made every decision that mattered. The USSR was the first managerial society; Nazi Germany, fascist Italy and New Deal America were the next. Burnham noted with some relish that President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1940 re-election campaign had stopped using the language of “businessmen” and “bankers” and instead had turned to phrases like “technicians in industry” and “managers.”

But Burnham was wrong about nearly everything that followed. These managerial superstates didn’t divide up the world. The United States and the Soviet Union instead allied against Germany. And by the 1980s America had reverted, with a convert’s enthusiasm, to the sanctity of private property — the one ideological development Burnham had explicitly ruled out, since he believed both private property and the ideas justifying it were on their way to extinction. Once communism collapsed in Eastern Europe, and capitalism seemed set to become the only game in town, the whole managerial thesis looked like a period curiosity, the sort of thing one cites to show how confidently intelligent people can misread their own moment.

Burnham may have been wrong about the political outcome, but he was asking the right question: Who controls the instruments of production, and what class does that control create? This is the only question that has ever reliably predicted anything about the structure of a society and its rulers. The managers did rise. But they didn’t rise against capital, expropriating it through the state. They rose into capital. They became capitalists themselves and, in doing so, produced something that neither Burnham nor Marx anticipated: a ruling class simultaneously at the top of the wage distribution and ownership distribution curve.

In “The Great Global Transformation,” one of us (Branko Milanovic) coined the term homoploutia to describe a new class of people who are equally or “samely” (homo) rich (ploutia) in both factors of production — that is, who are highly compensated both from their labor and from capital income. The emergence of the homoploutic class is arguably the most important structural change in capitalism since World War II. It is now about to be tested by a technology that is on the verge of completely rearranging the relationship between capital and labor.

It isn’t just the fact that today’s rich people work more than yesterday’s rich people did, as economist Thomas Piketty has observed. It’s that today’s richest people are both the highest-paid wage-earners and the richest capitalists. We define the homoploutic class as those in the top decile by labor income (e.g., salary), capital income (e.g. interest and dividends) and total income, and we find that roughly 30% of the top American income decile qualifies — that is, 3% of the total U.S. population. That share has risen steadily since the early 1980s, tracking almost exactly the rise in income inequality and the fall in intergenerational mobility.

Compare this to Mexico, where the homoploutia sits below 1% of the overall population. There, capitalism still runs on the classical pattern: the rich don’t work for a wage, and the well-paid doctors or lawyers don’t own enough property to reach the top decile of capitalists. The same holds in Brazil, Peru, Colombia. Richer countries fall in between — the homoploutic class in Spain, Italy, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden all cluster around 2-2.5% of the population. The United States is the most extreme case, which makes it a case worth studying.

As bad as inequality of income from labor is, it’s far more extreme when it comes to income from capital. When one considers capital income alone, the picture resolves into an almost feudal geometry. Sixty percent of American households have zero or negligible cash income from capital ownership. (That compares to 79% in Spain, 93% in Colombia and 96% in Peru as of 2021, according to Milanovic.) Income from capital is extraordinarily concentrated, with its Gini coefficient (an income-inequality measurement) about twice that of disposable income. The top 1% of American capitalists received nearly $100,000 per person in capital income in 2022, which for a household of four implies $400,000 a year from financial assets alone. This included interest, dividends, rents and privately funded pensions. The homoploutic class proper — that is, people in the top decile in both labor and capital income — earns about $20,548 per person, or north of $80,000 per family, from capital income. That may not be plutocratic money, but it is a solid floor beneath a very good salary. And the fusion of these incomes brings invulnerability.

A pure wage-earner is exposed to the labor market; a pure rentier is exposed to the stock market. The homoploutic household is exposed to both and therefore, in practice, to neither. A bad year for equities is cushioned by the salary; a lost job is cushioned by the portfolio. This is why we argue that homoploutia is arguably the only development in modern capitalism that would have surprised Marx. It doesn’t resolve the conflict between capital and labor by abolishing one side. It resolves it by locating both sides inside the same person. There is no class struggle in a household that draws from both factors — the struggle has been internalized and, thereby, essentially eliminated.

The homoploutic class has a sociological face and an ideological one as well. In “The Meritocracy Trap(2019),” the law professorDaniel Markovits described the class’s machinery: The elite is hard-working and credentialed and is therefore convinced that its position is earned — even as the value of parental investment separating an elite child as compared to a middle-class child by the end of graduate school is equivalent to a traditional inheritance in the neighborhood of $10 million per child. He calls merit “an ideological conceit, constructed to launder a fundamentally unjust allocation of advantage.” One can put it as a modification of Marx’s M–C–M’ (money-commodity-money) circuit: here the circuit becomes M–E–M’, where E is the education of one’s children. But if E gets out of reach for all but the children of homoplouts, it means that class mobility has effectively closed.

This isn’t a technocratic class in the sense that scholars like Jan Tinbergen, John Kenneth Galbraith, Raymond Aron or Clark Kerr meant in the 1960s, when they imagined East and West converging on the same efficient methods of administration, with managers indifferent to ownership structure. The homoploutic class is different precisely because its material interest and its ideological commitment to private property are the same thing. It defends capital because it is capital, and it defends educational credentials and labor because it is that too.

That double grounding in educational credentials and workplace performance has been the source of the class’s political legitimacy for decades. The message to everyone below was coherent, if irritating: We are rich because we are useful, because we have studied hard and worked hard, and you may join us if you are useful, too. Such a path was narrow and expensive, but it existed, and its existence did most of the ideological work.

Now what happens when we insert artificial intelligence into this structure?

Much is still unknown. We don’t know whether AI will raise our total labor output or merely shift production from human labor to machines without expanding the total. For example, dictating essays rather than typing them may allow people to write faster, but not necessarily more. (Generating good ideas turns out to be a rate-limiting factor.) The technology changed the composition of effort without changing the output; something similar may hold for AI. We also don’t know whether AI’s capabilities will continue to progress as rapidly and inexorably as its promoters promise, especially given the circular financing methods used for data centers and other computational capacity, and the political backlash against building them. Finally, we do not know how fast the technology will be adopted and integrated in productivity-enhancing ways.

But if we accept the premise that the technology will work roughly as its promoters claim, two very different futures open for the homoploutic class and thus for us as a society. The difference between these two scenarios turns on a specific and currently unresolved empirical question: whether AI will be a substitute for or a complement to high-premium cognitive labor. We cannot be certain which will prevail.

The first possible future is elite entrenchment. The homoploutic household earns a large salary and holds a diversified portfolio. As capital’s share of national income rises — because the quantity of capital rises with AI deployment while the average profit rate is held up by Schumpeterian destruction of the old capital stock — the portfolio leg of their income simply gets heavier. If they can hold onto their high-paying jobs, they can purchase shareholdings in exactly the sectors growing in the new economy. In this scenario, the homoploutic class thickens, from a third of the top labor-income decile to half or two-thirds. These elites can then continue to transmit their advantages to their offspring through education and inheritance, with even greater reliability, because now they have more of both to transmit. In this scenario, today’s top 3% of Americans becomes the stable, self-reproducing aristocracy of an AI economy. In the limit case, the top 10% of labor-income earners will also be the top 10% of capital-income earners, and they will lock in these same positions for their children, effectively creating a form of hardworking aristocracy. Homoploutia will have simply been a transitional state along the way to a renewed form of hereditary hierarchy.

The second alternate future is class dissolution. Homoplouts typically work jobs that command a wage premium in today’s labor market — as lawyers, financiers, consultants, software engineers, doctors and so on — because they require cognitive work often enabled by fancy educations, diplomas and credentials. Unfortunately for these individuals, this is also precisely the sort of work that large language models perform most convincingly. As the roboticist Hans Moravec famously observed, high-level reasoning turns out to be easier to automate than sensorimotor skills developed over a billion years of evolution.

If AI ends up substituting for rather than complementing knowledge work, then the wage premium commanded by highly educated workers will shrink. For such workers, the salary that complemented the income from their investment portfolio will diminish or disappear; what will remain is their portfolio alone. The homoploutic household in this case reverts to a purely capitalist household that lives entirely off the earnings from its investment portfolio; in other words, it reverts to Mexico’s classical pattern where the rich don’t work.

Under either scenario, the ideological position of the homoploutic class as a legitimate meritocracy will collapse. Under entrenchment, the homoploutic claim to merit becomes untenable because there is no path to entry: Once inheritance is the only way into the top decile of capitalists, such a class can’t credibly describe itself as meritocratic, no matter how hard-working. Under dissolution, if education no longer commands a wage premium, there is no longer any meritorious activity to point at — one is simply an owner of capital, as one’s great-grandfather was. In the first case the asset value of the class survives, but the flow into it stops. In the second, both go.

Around this reduced elite the rest of society’s structure becomes legible. At the summit we find the few thousand people who own the models. Next is the homoploutic remnant — thinned or thickened but closed to the lower ranks. Below them is a service class doing what AI cannot yet do, at low to moderate wages: think gardeners, home nursing aides, bartenders, tradesmen, mechanics and so on. These people will be employed, but not in any meaningful sense middle class. And finally, at the bottom sits a redundant population — the term “unemployed” is misleading, because it suggests a temporary state and a return path. The redundant or surplus population are people whose skills have been rendered obsolete, whose retraining would take years and that no one will fund. In theory, a universal basic income or a permanent unemployment benefit would solve their material problem, and perhaps such people can be kept pacified with religion, sex and TV. “Bread and circuses” is, after all, a venerable political solution; more than a few in Silicon Valley dream of UBI and TikTok memes as its modern update.

What is striking about this pyramid is its pre-industrial (that is, feudal) shape: sharply graded at the top, flat and wide at the bottom, with no substantial middle. Every society before the Industrial Revolution looked like this, and the 20th-century assumption that development produces a large middle class, which in turn produces political stability and democratic peace, was an inference from a period that may prove to have been exceptional. If AI creates such a rigid class pyramid, then the richest and most technologically advanced societies on Earth may well become politically more turbulent than poorer ones — a tragicomic inversion of modernization theory’s teleological belief in the coming universalization of stably democratic middle-class societies. A large lumpen population with little stable work or social status (and unlimited free time) represents a reserve army of politically combustible malcontents — ready kindling for political operators with a grievance and a budget.

A hierarchy that can be scaled, even improbably, is a hierarchy that at least potentially can be tolerated, even within a democracy. For much of the last century, inequality was justified with the claim that some people were more talented and hardworking than others, a process that educational institutions vouched for through an elaborately formalized ranking and credentialing system. This is the meritocracy, and homoplouts are the No. 1 beneficiaries of this ideology. A closed-off hierarchy, however, is intolerable to a democracy. This helps to explain why so many in Silicon Valley are moving in a markedly and explicitly anti-democratic direction — the subject of Gil Duran’s recently published “The Nerd Reich.”

The Roman analogy is relevant here for reasons that go beyond our tech elites’ decadence. The late Republic didn’t fall because the masses rose spontaneously in revolt against the elites. It fell because the oligarchic clans couldn’t settle their disputes among themselves and each faction found it expedient to mobilize the idle urban population against its rivals. A socioeconomic structure with a handful of enormously wealthy factions at the top and a large supported-but-purposeless population at the bottom doesn’t require a revolutionary movement to become unstable. It requires only that one plutocrat decide his interests are better served by mobilizing the malcontents rather than parleying with his peers.

Burnham was wrong in predicting that managers would displace capitalists: the “shareholder value” revolution of the 1970s-1980s dethroned the postwar managerial class and ensured that corporations would place the interests of capital ahead of all other stakeholders. But he was right to insist that the instruments of production are the seat of social domination, that whoever controls them controls society, and that ideology follows from this rather than determining it. He grounded both capitalist and managerial society in the relations of production, which is why the recent enthusiasm for enlisting him in arguments about a “woke” professional-managerial class is either a misunderstanding or a misappropriation. Burnham wasn’t writing about the opinions of the credentialed. He was writing about the people who control the machines.

Applied to our moment, his question — Who controls the instruments of production, and what class does that control create? — is discomfiting. If artificial intelligence becomes the decisive instrument of modern production, then those who control it become the new ruling class. Educational credentials as such will no longer work to legitimate society’s socioeconomic hierarchy. The homoplouts may end up being the last generation of a ruling class that was required to be good at something other than clipping coupons. Or some small fraction of them may end up as the owners of the machines that replaced them, which is a different fate but not, in the long run, a more legitimate one.

All we are reasonably sure of is that the roughly 40-year settlement in which the same people held the best jobs and the most property — and pointed to the first as justification for the second — is coming to an end in one way or another. Advocates of abundance who imagine machines doing the work while we enjoy our leisure have described the economics correctly and the politics not at all. We may well get abundance. But what we won’t get on present trajectories is a society organized in a way that anyone outside of the ultra-elite would want.

title: Clark resigns as Hartlepool boss in post-match interview
description: Lee Clark resigns as Hartlepool United head coach after a sixth loss in seven games following the 3-1 home defeat by Worthing.
fullText:
Lee Clark resigned as Hartlepool United head coach with immediate effect following their home defeat by Worthing.

The 3-1 loss was a third defeat in a row and a sixth in seven matches, pushing Pools down to 18th before the afternoon kick-offs in the National League.

Clark took over at Victoria Park in the summer after a short spell with Rotherham United at the end of last season, but fans called for his head during Saturday's game as Hartlepool's slump continued.

"I resign from my position with immediate effect," Clark, a former Newcastle, Sunderland and Fulham player, told BBC Radio Tees.

"I wanted to give this club and the fans something to be proud of, what they deserve, but I haven't been able to do that unfortunately."

The former Huddersfield Town and Birmingham City boss added: "I was excited to take the job and I wanted to be the man to get them back to where they need to be and deserve to be, but it hasn't worked out."

Pools were taken over in January by American businessman Landon Smith as the County Durham club aim to end their four-year stay in the National League.

But the search now begins for their ninth permanent manager or head coach in this period outside the English Football League.

title: Blaze win One-Day Cup in last-ball thriller
description: Emma Jones seals the Blaze's treble success with a dramatic last-ball boundary to win a thrilling One-Day Cup final and shatter Hampshire's hopes of silverware.
fullText:
Emma Jones sealed The Blaze's treble success with a dramatic last-ball boundary to win a thrilling One-Day Cup final and shatter Hampshire's hopes of silverware.

The Blaze, who had already won the T20 Blast and County Cup trophies this season, seemed to be coasting towards their target of 252 after half-centuries from Tammy Beaumont (74) and Georgia Elwiss (64) at the Utilita Bowl.

But Hampshire's spinners fought back, with Amanda-Jade Wellington taking 3-36 and Bex Tyson 2-46 as four wickets went down for 29 to leave the Blaze needing 30 from the final three overs.

However, Jones kept her cool with an unbeaten 34 from 25 balls and, with two still required from Daisy Gibb's final delivery, pulled it to the boundary to clinch a remarkable treble for her side.

That meant heartbreak for Hampshire on home soil for a second successive year, having lost the 2025 final to Lancashire.

Asked to bat after Blaze captain Kirstie Gordon won the toss, Hampshire started slowly but Ella McCaughan and Maia Bouchier gradually eased into their rhythm to share an opening stand of 84 from 106.

Women's One-Day Cup final: Blaze seal dramatic win over Hampshire with final ball of match

Bouchier, who had hit hundreds in both of her past two innings, took a liking to the bowling of Lucy Higham, driving the off-spinner twice for leg-side boundaries – but then she tried to do it a third time and picked out the long-on fielder.

Hampshire skipper Georgia Adams departed cheaply, smacking Higham's full toss to mid-off, but McCaughan eased past her half-century as Freya Kemp seized control, hitting the spinners cleanly over the top and smashing Higham for the first six of the innings.

However, having reached 166-2, Hampshire began to stutter as Grace Ballinger returned for a second spell to trap McCaughan lbw for 78 and Kemp (52 from 46) was lured down the track by Higham (4-49) and stumped.

Wickets continued to tumble as Charley Phillips (3-38) struck three times in rapid succession and Gordon, whose consistent 10 overs cost just 39, produced an outstanding one-handed catch at mid-on to remove Naomi Dattani.

Gibb and Poppy Tulloch did just enough to haul Hampshire above the 250 mark in the final over of the innings, but their hopes of capturing early wickets in the Blaze response proved forlorn.

Beaumont struck back-to-back fours off Dattani to raise the 50 partnership well before the end of the powerplay and Adams went for 13 in her second over as Sarah Bryce walloped her high over the long-on boundary.

It was Wellington who raised Hampshire spirits by dismissing both Bryce sisters in the same over, with Sarah sweeping to deep square leg before Kathryn was brilliantly taken by Adams at slip, leaping low to her left.

Elwiss provided a calming influence, milking singles and rotating the strike effectively with the former England batter, who passed 50 from 75, albeit riding her luck at times with some aerial shots and risky singles.

The opener was put down by Kemp, diving forward at deep midwicket, while Rhianna Southby missed a stumping chance off Tyson soon afterwards – but Beaumont's good fortune eventually ran out when Wellington landed one bang on her left foot and in front.

Elwiss, who brought up her 50 with successive fours off Wellington, then took up the baton – but The Blaze still needed 51 when she fell to Tyson, whose spell of 2-46 helped to stifle the batters as boundaries dried up almost entirely.

Hampshire looked favourites, only for Jones to take two fours off the penultimate over from Dattani and, despite the run-out of Higham with three required, her composure was enough to guide the Blaze home.

title: Frenetic draw with Canada ends England's 39-game winning run
description: England's remarkable winning run comes to an end as they are held to a nail-biting 26-26 draw by Canada at Sandy Park.
fullText:
Tries: Moloney-MacDonald 2, Botterman, Field Cons: Harrison 3

Tries: Gibson, Menin 2 Cons: De Goede 3

England's remarkable 39-match winning run came to an end as they were held to a nail-biting 26-26 draw by Canada at Sandy Park.

The Red Roses were unable to escape the clutches of a relentless Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, with the two sides sharing four tries apiece in front of a raucous 14,573 crowd in Exeter.

Canada are the first team to avoid defeat against England since New Zealand beat them in the 2022 World Cup final, but John Mitchell's side are now unbeaten in 40 Tests.

The draw also ended England's 100% home record against Canada, having won each of their previous 13 home meetings.

In a pulsating opening 25 minutes, England were twice required to come from behind, with tries from Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Hannah Botterman cancelling out scores by Lizzie Gibson and DaLeaka Menin for Canada.

Exeter winger Moloney-MacDonald had a try disallowed before giving England the lead for the first time in the 32nd minute, getting on the end of a surging run from Sadia Kabeya for her second of the match.

However, Canada - who had earlier had a brilliant solo effort from Asia Hogan-Rochester chalked off for a forward pass - hit back on the stroke of half-time when Menin crashed over from close range.

England weathered 10 minutes of sustained pressure at the beginning of the second half before the two sides exchanged tries again, prop Bryony Field restoring the lead for the hosts before Canada scrum-half Olivia Apps scored under the posts after a dancing run from Sophie de Goede down the left wing.

England looked the most likely to win in a chaotic final 10 minutes, including being held up over the line, but were left to a rue a turnover in front of the posts and a loose carry as Canada battled through for the draw.

The two sides will resume their rivalry with two Tests in Canada in October.

Before then, England face New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday, 26 September.

England's run of 39 consecutive wins, which started in March 2023, encompassed four successive Women's Six Nations crowns, two WXV1 successes and a home World Cup triumph in 2025.

But all things must come to an end.

It is not that England have not been tested in that time. A week earlier, Australia led 10-5 at half-time, marking the first time the Red Roses had trailed at the interval since 2020.

France have often been a thorn in their side in Six Nations deciders too, while Canada ran them close in a WXV meeting in 2024.

The challenge for opponents has been sustaining that pressure for a full 80-minute performance, and Canada did not let up at Sandy Park.

Twice they led, twice they were pegged back. There was an ominous feeling when Moloney-MacDonald put the hosts in front, but Canada seized their opportunity, capitalising on back-to-back penalties in England's 22 to level.

On the back foot as England - energised by their replacements - pressed for the win, they responded twice more, first cancelling out Field's try and then doggedly defending in their own half for much of the final 20 minutes.

As impressive as Canada were in defence, England were also left to rue the lack of a clinical touch in Canada's 22 and opted against kicking for three points when awarded a penalty in the closing stages.

But rather than be disappointed, head coach Mitchell hailed the opportunity that the result presents.

"Canada were good and we were also good," he said. "At times it was a real arm wrestle.

"We are really in a Test series, which is great for us. Canada need to be congratulated on their performance.

"For us, it's about getting better and there is a greater purpose than just one Test match. This is ideal for us and allows us to stay focused on what's necessary to get a better performance."

Speaking before the match, Canada captain De Goede said recollections of last year's World Cup final defeat has kept her awake "four to five nights a week".

Even after snapping the world champions' record unbeaten run, De Goede contemplated what might have been.

"There's definitely some frustration that we didn't get the win in the end, but also we're moving in the right direction from the last time we played them," said the second row forward.

"We need to be critical of ourselves after the game because I do think we could have got the win.

"We know we can get it across the line and that's where the disappointment comes from. There's a lot of pride in our defensive stance in the last 20 minutes, but we really struggled to exit, so we'll have to watch back what we were doing on the attacking side of the ball."

With the clock in the red, Canada had a scrum near to their own 22 and De Goede said the players on the field were keen to keep the game alive, but afterwards the skipper reluctantly conceded that coach Kevin Rouet made the right call by instructing them to kick to touch and end the match.

"The plan on the field - we were like 'let's go for the win'," said De Goede. "Then the message came on from the sideline to kick it out.

"I do trust Kevin, he has the cooler head in that moment. If we gave away a penalty off the next breakdown, we'd be sitting here going 'why didn't you kick it out?'"

Replacements: Campbell, Carson, Bern, Burns, Feaunati, M Packer, Robinson, Aitchison.

title: Suzuki proves worthy replacement for Martinez at Villa
description: Aston Villa new boy Zion Suzuki deserves as much credit as anyone for their first Premier League win of the season at struggling Tottenham.
fullText:
While Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson both scored, another Aston Villa new boy, Zion Suzuki, deserved as much credit as anyone for their first Premier League win of the season at struggling Tottenham.

The Japan goalkeeper made the move to Villa from Italian side Parma for a fee in the region of £30m in August.

And his performance against Spurs suggests he is more than capable of filling the very big boots vacated by the departure of Argentina number one - and fan favourite - Emiliano Martinez to Chelsea.

In particular, his two saves from Savio within seconds of each other and a moment of good fortune when Archie Gray's effort clipped wide off his foot, gave Villa the platform to ride out a period in the game when the hosts held sway.

"We needed the keeper," said Villa boss Unai Emery in his post-match interviews.

"He is a keeper to save us. To make sure in the goal he has the quality and then he has the skills to play and build up.

"It is very important how he is doing it and sometimes taking some risks, but through those he is improving and learning."

One of the attractions around signing the 24-year-old in August was his apparent assuredness with the ball at his feet and his ability to spray the ball forward with very little backlift.

And on a day when things could not have gone much better for him, Suzuki ended up as the architect of Villa's second goal, with his booming ball forward from his own six-yard box dropping deep into Tottenham territory, where Jackson collected it and dispatched an unerring shot to the left corner.

"In the build up, he can choose to play long balls because he has a very long pass in behind and he did that for the second goal we scored," added Emery.

Villa survive late Spurs fightback to earn first Premier League win

No revival in sight for 'fragile' Spurs after Villa defeat

Born in the United States to a Ghanaian father and a Japanese mother, Suzuki has already played in Japan, Belgium and Italy and won 28 caps for his country.

And speaking to BBC Sport in August, Dennis Rudel - his former coach at Sint-Truiden - stressed that Suzuki has the attributes to become one of the world's best in his position.

"It is possible if he stays healthy," said the former Union Berlin coach. "With his physical strength, there is no-one better in the world in terms of dynamic, jumping power, throws and kicking the ball.

"When I watched him at the World Cup [for Japan], his biggest strength was his mental clearness. His focus on the game or in training sessions is so good. He is always prepared and really disciplined.

"He is aiming to show he can be one of the best. He was immediately one of the top four or five goalkeepers in Serie A.

"As a person and as a player, he is a role model for how you should behave. I don't see any weakness in him."

"He has such big hands and he is powerful. When he can reach the ball, it is a 90-95% chance of a save. It is something really special."
