title: 'Fragile' Tottenham beaten by Aston Villa despite late rally
description: The end to Tottenham's Premier League goal drought came too late as Aston Villa won 3-2 in north London on Saturday to compound a miserable start for Roberto De Zerbi's men.Without a league win this season, Tottenham are off to their worst start in the Premier League era and only netted their first goals of the campaign after the visitors had surged into a 3-0 lead.
fullText:
The end to Tottenham's Premier League goal drought came too late as Aston Villa won 3-2 in north London on Saturday to compound a miserable start for Roberto De Zerbi's men.

Without a league win this season, Tottenham are off to their worst start in the Premier League era and only netted their first goals of the campaign after the visitors had surged into a 3-0 lead.

Villa had also struggled for goals themselves since the side that won the Europa League last season was torn apart during the transfer window.

But new signings Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson struck either side of half-time before Emi Buendia's wonder strike to give Unai Emery's new-look team their first league win.

"Competing like we did, winning like we did will give us confidence collectively and individually, it is really very important," said Emery.

"We are delighted because we needed it and we were suffering in the Premier League."

Even Tottenham's first late consolation needed the aid of a Villa deflection when Conor Gallagher's effort went in off Matty Cash before Jan Paul van Hecke headed home in stoppage time.

Spurs splashed out over £300 million ($400 million) on new players to try and avoid a repeat of the battle for survival they endured last season.

Yet there remains little return on that investment.

"I want to say is that we played well in the first half, we didn't score, but (we are ) too fragile," said De Zerbi.

"The moment when we have to defend, we have to defend compact. The leaders have to be leaders and to lead the team."

In keeping with recent performances, Spurs started brightly before fizzling out.

Twice in a matter of seconds Savio was kept out by Suzuki before the Japanese goalkeeper spread himself to turn behind Archie Gray's powerful strike.

Villa had picked up just one point from their opening four league games but have missed their club record signing Manzambi for most of that period.

The Swiss international opened his Villa account when he tapped home Boubacar Kamara's cross.

De Zerbi described Tottenham's defending for the second goal as "incredible" and not in a good sense as Van Hecke failed to deal with a long ball straight down the middle.

Jackson did well to evade the Dutch defender and then fired down into the ground and past Antonin Kinsky.

The Czech goalkeeper was powerless to stop Villa's third 11 minutes from time when Buendia took aim from long range and brilliantly picked out the top corner.

A chorus of boos greeted Buendia's strike as thousands of home fans headed for an early exit.

But those that left missed finally have something to celebrate.

Fine persistence from Mohammed Kudus teed up Gallagher to find the bottom corner via the outstretched foot of Cash.

Van Hecke then bulleted in from Andy Robertson's free-kick with virtually the last touch of the game.

Spurs now must stew on another defeat for a three-week international break while rooted in the relegation zone.

Villa, by contrast, will hope victory can prove the catalyst to storm up the table as they did last season.

Emery's men failed to win any of their first five league games a year ago, but ultimately finished fourth.

title: Sixers' Jaylen Brown working out with new assistant coach Phil Handy
description: Philadelphia 76ers star Jaylen Brown got some work in with new assistant coach Phil Handy in the gym.
fullText:
The Philadelphia 76ers have a number of new pieces that need to be integrated into an already solid nucleus. The Sixers were able to make some noise in the 2025-26 season as they finished with 47 wins, then rallied from a 3-1 deficit to eliminate the Boston Celtics in Round 1, before falling short to the New York Knicks in Round 2.

The Sixers then had a home run of a summer as they made a couple of big moves early in free agency, swung a deal to acquire Jaylen Brown from the Celtics, then landed LeBron James and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, before then hiring Phil Handy to be the team's assistant coach.

Handy has a ton of history with members of the Sixers as he has won titles with James with the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2016 and Los Angeles Lakers in 2020. He also won a title with the Toronto Raptors in 2019 as an assistant under the guidance of coach Nick Nurse.

description: West Ham United player Taty Castellanos has been accused of spitting at Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall during Saturday’s derby at The Den.The incident happened in the 65th minute of the game wh...
fullText:
West Ham United player Taty Castellanos has been accused of spitting at Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall during Saturday's derby at The Den.

The incident happened in the 65th minute of the game when Marschall kept hold of the ball longer than the allotted six seconds while the hosts were leading 2-0.

Castellanos came flying across in a bid to close the 23-year-old goalkeeper down.

Players from both teams were involved in a melee in no time.

Marschall then appeared to point towards his jersey, gesturing that he had been spat at by Castellanos.

Sky Sports reported that the fourth official confirmed an allegation of spitting had been lodged by Millwall staff.

The Lions dominated the first half of the derby and scored goals through Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli.

But West Ham produced a stunning comeback after the break to earn a share in the spoils.

Substitute Mohamadou Kante pulled one back with a low strike from 25 yards in the 74th minute.

Then Konstantinos Mavropanos headed home the equaliser six minutes later.

Kante received a red card for pulling down Millwall's Kyrell Lisbie, but the Hammers held on to secure a draw.

West Ham have made a positive start to the Championship season, as they aim for an immediate return to the Premier League.

The Irons have picked up 15 points from eight matches and are currently at the top of the league table. Although teams below them will likely overtake them after their matches this weekend.

title: Tom Brady: It's time to begin Bears QB Caleb Williams' MVP campaign
description: Former Super Bowl legend Tom Brady proclaimed it's time to begin the MVP campaign for Bears quarterback Caleb Williams.
fullText:
Add NFL legend, Super Bowl champion, and FOX broadcaster Tom Brady to the growing list of those who are buying in on Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams.

Although it is just one week, Williams has made plenty of fans across the league after his performance in the Week 1 win over the Carolina Panthers, where he completed 21-of-29 passes for 269 yards and two touchdowns while adding 65 rushing yards and two rushing scores in a dominant offensive showing.

Earlier this week, Brady revealed his top five power rankings heading into week two of the NFL season. And not only did he have the Bears in second place, he also said it's time to start the clock for Caleb Williams MVP campaign.

"The Caleb Williams MVP watch is underway," Brady said. "The Bears are No. 2 (in his power rankings), they put 59 (points) on Carolina in Week 1, Ben Johnson wants the highest scoring offense ever, but we need to see a little defense from this team when they get back to Chicago. Or you know what, screw it, keep scoring 59 points, I'm an offensive guy, either way works."

It's incredible to see all the names of analysts who are buying in on Williams this season, but last week was just the beginning, and he'll have to continue to build on that. Regardless, hearing the man that many believe to be the greatest quarterback of all-time, love him or hate him, compliment the Bears quarterback, it doesn't get much better in terms of hype.

title: Tottenham's damning Arsenal comparison shows how bad things have got for Spurs and Roberto De Zerbi
description: Tottenham's loss to Aston Villa means they go into the international break in the relegation zone.
fullText:
Tottenham's damning Arsenal comparison shows how bad things have got for Spurs and Roberto De Zerbi originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Tottenham Hotspur have endured a miserable start to the 2026-27 season, and things got worse in their final game before the extended international break.

Spurs found themselves 3-0 down at home to Aston Villa on Saturday, prompting thousands of fans to head for the exits following goals from Johan Manzambi, Nicolas Jackson, and Emi Buendia. Although they got two late goals, ending their long wait to score in the top flight, they still ended up on the wrong end of a 3-2 scoreline.

The result means Roberto De Zerbi's team will be in the relegation zone when the Premier League returns on October 10. Spurs will face Manchester United at Old Trafford that weekend.

Perhaps returning to league action away from home will not be a bad thing for De Zerbi and his players given their remarkably poor record at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

MORE:Latest Premier League news and standings show Spurs already struggling

Spurs' loss to Aston Villa was their 50th defeat in 141 league matches at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which staged its first game in April 2019.

That means more than 35 per cent of their league games at their impressive home venue have ended in defeat. What's more, they have lost 22 home league fixtures since the start of 2024-25, having lost only 23 in all four of the previous seasons combined.

50 - Tottenham Hotspur have lost 50 of their 141 Premier League games at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, as many defeats as Arsenal have suffered in 382 top-flight matches at the Emirates Stadium.

Gap. pic.twitter.com/M9bGo0HEPk

Even more damning is the comparison with arch-rivals Arsenal. The Gunners have lost the same number of league games at their home, Emirates Stadium, but in 382 total matches over the course of 20 years.

Arsenal very much boast the north London bragging rights at the moment, and this further highlights the disparity between these two teams right now. It's horrible reading for the Spurs faithful.

While Gallagher and Van Hecke finally ended Spurs' wait for league goals, they could not prevent this result setting another unwanted record.

Two points and a goal difference of -6 is the club's worst start to a Premier League season after five matches, surpassing 2008/09, when they managed two points and a goal difference of -3.

That season saw Juande Ramos sacked as manager in October after winning just two of 12 games in all competitions. Harry Redknapp took over and steered them to an eighth-place finish in the top flight, and the final of the EFL Cup, which they lost to Manchester United.

De Zerbi said after the match that Spurs were "too fragile" after falling behind against the run of play while Micky van de Ven was being treated for a facial injury, having tested Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki in the first half.

"I think we could score in the first half many, many times," he said to TNT Sports. "We concede a goal with 10 players, but we had to stay more focused to defend that situation in extra time in the first half. In the second half, we concede a goal from a goal-kick directly. Before then, we score and it's offside. The third goal is a great goal of Buendia.

"What you want I have to say? We played well in the first half. We didn't score. But [we are] too fragile.

"If [we] don't score, it's my responsibility. I take my responsibility. Football is like life: you are stronger, or you lose.

"I can't speak [about] before my time [at the club], I can just speak about my work. We have to improve the quality of the play, but to be stronger, wiser. The game is not 90 minutes of ball possession, 90 minutes in the last third. There are situations when we have to stay closer, when we have to stay stronger, we have to defend better, ball on ball, and we didn't, or we didn't in the right way."

title: Adrian Peterson Completes Court-Ordered Community Service in Minnesota DWI Case
description: Adrian Peterson has completed the community-service requirement imposed after his 2025 Minnesota DWI arrest. The former NFL MVP logged enough hours in July to satisfy ... Read More
fullText:
Adrian Peterson has completed the community-service requirement imposed after his 2025 Minnesota DWI arrest.

The former NFL MVP logged enough hours in July to satisfy the 32 hours ordered by the court, according to documents obtained by TMZ. The records show Peterson performed the work between July 13 and July 30.

His service included four-hour shifts with Meals on Wheels and a local food drive, along with work involving bags for homeless youth, a YMCA program and an event for senior citizens.

Completing those hours moves Peterson closer to resolving the Minnesota case, but community service was only one component of the sentence he received after pleading guilty earlier this year. His other conditions included a stayed jail sentence, a victim impact panel and restrictions tied to his probation.

Peterson pleaded guilty in March to one count of driving while impaired. Court documents showed that he received a 90-day sentence at the Hennepin County Adult Corrections Facility, but the jail term was stayed for one year as long as he complied with the court's conditions.

He was ordered to complete 32 hours of community service within 180 days and attend a victim impact panel. Peterson was also required to undergo an alcohol screening, which court records indicated he had already completed by the time the plea agreement was reported. The remaining charges were dismissed as part of the deal, according to TMZ.

The agreement also required Peterson to avoid alcohol- or drug-related offenses and reckless-driving offenses during the one-year period in which the jail sentence was stayed.

The case began in the early hours of April 25, 2025, after Peterson appeared at the Minnesota Vikings' NFL Draft event at U.S. Bank Stadium. A Minnesota State Patrol trooper stopped his Audi Q5 in Richfield at about 3:20 a.m. after seeing it travel 83 mph in a 55-mph zone.

A preliminary breath test measured Peterson's blood alcohol concentration at 0.14%, according to authorities. Minnesota's legal driving limit is 0.08%.

Peterson was booked into the Hennepin County Jail at 5:16 a.m. and released just over two hours later after posting $4,000 bond, the Associated Press reported.

Peterson's guilty plea addressed the charge stemming from the Minnesota stop, but he was arrested again on suspicion of DWI in Texas later in 2025.

Police in Sugar Land arrested Peterson in October after finding him asleep behind the wheel of a vehicle at a gas station, according to court records later reported by Reuters. Officers said the vehicle's engine was running and that Peterson showed signs of intoxication.

Police also reported finding a handgun inside the glove compartment, resulting in an additional charge of unlawfully carrying a weapon. Peterson was released from the Fort Bend County Jail on $3,000 bond.

title: Lane Kiffin showered with boos, expletive-laden chants in 'College GameDay' interview
description: Lane Kiffin joined 'College GameDay' ahead of his LSU team's game at Ole Miss. Here's how Rebels fans reacted to their now-former coach
fullText:
Within two seconds of Lane Kiffin appearing on the video board on the "College GameDay" set in a white LSU shirt, the boos began.

And that was just the beginning.

More: College football bold predictions: Week 3 upset picks include LSU

In the hours before Kiffin returns to Vaught-Hemingway Stadium to face off against the Mississippi program he coached the previous six seasons, he joined "GameDay" virtually from what appeared to be a hotel ballroom for an interview about one of the most eagerly anticipated games of the 2026 college football season.

The thousands of Ole Miss fans gathered in The Grove didn't wait long to let their former coach know how they felt about him. Kiffin was almost immediately greeted with boos before chants of "[Expletive] Lane Kiffin" echoed from the crowd, which continued for a handful of minutes.

The Ole Miss crowd's reaction to Lane Kiffin's appearance on College GameDay: pic.twitter.com/OVTxQTvfKK

Later on in the five-minute hit, fans shifted their focus to a different expletive, referring to Kiffin in chant as the orifice out of which creatures defecate.

Only 10 months ago, Kiffin was an icon to many of the people assembled in Oxford, Mississippi on Saturday, leading Ole Miss to a 55-19 mark in six seasons. His final team went 11-1 in the 2025 regular season, earning it a spot in the College Football Playoff.

Before the playoff began, though, Kiffin left the Rebels for rival LSU, where he agreed to a seven-year, $91 million contract. Without Kiffin, and under the watch of new head coach Pete Golding, Ole Miss won two games to advance to the playoff semifinals, where it lost, 31-27, to eventual national runner-up Miami.

Kiffin's first LSU team enters Saturday's Week 3 matchup with the Rebels at 2-0, with lopsided wins over Clemson and Louisiana Tech that have put it at No. 7 in the US LBM Coaches Poll. Ole Miss, meanwhile, is two spots behind at No. 9 and features arguably the best quarterback-running back pairing in college football in Trinidad Chambliss and Kewan Lacy, both of whom stayed with the Rebels rather than follow Kiffin.

title: Nick Saban explains why Ohio State lost its edge at half vs. Texas
description: Nick Saban explains why Ohio State lost its edge and momentum during a second half collapse against Texas.
fullText:
Former Alabama football coach Nick Saban said he knew exactly why Ohio State's momentum at halftime disappeared in the second half against Texas, which led to a 20-point comeback from the Longhorns in their 24-23 win.

"I think the big thing from Ohio State, and I've been through this before: you get ahead at halftime, they score right before the half. The players are all smiling, and they're all thinking 'We got this.' You lose your edge when you do that," Saban said on ESPN's "College Gameday."

The Buckeyes were up 20-3 at half against Texas and also received the first possession of the second half. Texas struggled to get started against Ohio State, with its first two offensive possessions resulting in turnovers that led to Ohio State scores.

But in the second half, Ohio State's execution crumbled on both offense and defense while the Longhorns gained momentum.

"I used to take little notes because I wanted to know whose [expletive] I could chew out at halftime," Saban said. "But no scoreboard at halftime. .... When you lose your edge in the game, you lose the momentum and it's really hard to get it back, and that's exactly what happened."

As a result of the loss, Ohio State fell from No. 1 to No. 6 in the US LBM Coaches poll and the Associated Press poll. Texas climbed to the top spot in each poll.

title: Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu sets attendance world record for a youth match in U20 Intercontinental Cup
description: As reported by AS, Real Madrid’s stadium, the Santiago Bernabeu has made history today when it hosted the U20 Intercontinental Cup final.A total of 52,117 spectators attended the meeting between Rea...
fullText:
As reported by AS, Real Madrid's stadium, the Santiago Bernabeu has made history today when it hosted the U20 Intercontinental Cup final.

A total of 52,117 spectators attended the meeting between Real Madrid and Santiago Wanderers in the U20 Intercontinental Cup, setting a new world record for attendance at a youth football match.

What made the occasion even more special is that Real Madrid Juvenil A went on to win the match 3-1 and lift the Intercontinental Cup trophy after a chaotic final at the iconic stadium.

The attendance figure is significantly higher than the previous record, which was set during the Flamengo vs Barcelona match at the Maracana in 2025. That game attracted 45,656 spectators.

The Bernabeu therefore surpassed the previous mark by 6,461 fans, an increase of 14.2%.

Real Madrid Juvenil A won the U20 Intercontinental Cup. (Picture credit: X/@lafabricacrm)

The gap is even greater compared with the other recent editions of the tournament.

In 2022, Benfica vs Peñarol at Montevideo's Estadio Centenario drew 40,579 spectators. The following year, Boca Juniors vs AZ Alkmaar at La Bombonera attracted 37,386.

The lowest attendance came in 2024, when Flamengo vs Olympiacos at the Maracana drew 31,237 fans.

In comparison, the Bernabeu attendance figure was more than 20,800 higher, representing an increase of 66.8%.

The latest attendance is also around 35% higher than the average of the previous four editions, which stood at approximately 38,700 spectators per match.

Real Madrid's Juvenil A setup, managed by Alvaro Lopez, went on to lift the U20 Intercontinental Cup at the Santiago Bernabeu by beating Santiago Wanderers.

The Merengues' youth team entered the final as reigning UEFA Youth League champions after defeating Club Brugge in May, while Santiago Wanderers had earned their place by winning the Copa Libertadores at the same age level.

Daniel Yanez gave the hosts the lead before the South American outfit equalised after the break through Christian Silva despite being down to ten men.

Substitute Fran Santamaria handed Real Madrid the lead again in the 81st minute, making it 2-1, before Santiago Wanderers lost the plot and saw two more players get sent off, leaving them with only eight players on the field.

Roberto Martin then added the third for Real Madrid deep into stoppage time to kill the tie and secure the trophy for his team.

title: Zelensky thanks Trump for signing 'critically important' Russia sanctions bill
description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday thanked President Donald Trump for signing into law a bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, which allows for the expansion of sanctions on Russia related to Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump signed the bill on Friday, the White House said in a statement, after the legislation passed both the House and Senate with strong bipartisan backing. The legislation "authorizes and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran," the White House said.
The bill's passage came about two months after Graham died suddenly following a tear in his aorta.
fullText:
Trump signed the legislation into law on Friday, the White House said.

LONDON -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday thanked President Donald Trump for signing into law a bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, which allows for the expansion of sanctions on Russia related to Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Trump signed the bill on Friday, the White House said in a statement, after the legislation passed both the House and Senate with strong bipartisan backing. The legislation "authorizes and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran," the White House said.

The bill's passage came about two months after Graham died suddenly following a tear in his aorta. Graham had long been an advocate of U.S. support for Kyiv and more stringent measures on Russia and the regime headed by President Vladimir Putin. In 2024, Russia's state financial monitoring agency added Graham to its list of alleged "terrorists and extremists."

In a post to Telegram on Friday night, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for signing what he called "critically important legislation," extending his thanks to "all the senators and members of the House of Representatives who supported it."

"When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions and seek a path to peace," Zelenskyy wrote.

"In particular, in those capitals that choose to buy Russian oil, provide financial services to Russia, and allow Russian companies linked to Putin and the war to engage in normal business relations in other countries," he added.

"The best way to honor Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly. And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace. Peace -- and an end to all the problems and challenges this war has brought," the Ukrainian president wrote.

"Peace comes through strength. Calm comes through security. And the best guarantee of security is resolve," he added.

The legislation allows for primary and secondary sanctions on Russia and other countries that support Moscow in its invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year with no sign of a breakthrough in peace talks.

The sanctions target Russian political officials and oligarchs, banks and financial institutions, and Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" -- hundreds of tankers used to evade sanctions -- according to the bill.

The legislation allows for the president to impose tariffs, but limits the scope of those tariffs to the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas and the top five countries that aid Russia's energy sanctions evasion.

It also includes a provision to prevent a lapse in sanction authority that restricts funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

Russian officials hit out at the new legislation, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov telling reporters on Friday, "The introduction of any additional sanctions by the United States will definitely complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine."

Dmitry Medvedev -- the former Russian president and prime minister now serving as the deputy chairman of the country's Security Council -- described the legislation as an example of "Russophobic outrages" in a post to his Telegram channel on Saturday morning, before referring to Graham as a "dead terrorist."

The bill passed the House by a 262 to 159 vote. The legislation split House Democrats, with 58 voting in favor while 152 voted against. Seven Republican lawmakers joined the dissenting Democrats.

The Senate approved the measure last month with overwhelming bipartisan support by a vote of 86 to 11.

Top House Democratic leaders, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, explained why they voted against the sanctions bill, saying it "gives extraordinary power to Donald Trump."

ABC News' Michelle Stoddart, Rashid Haddou and Lauren Peller contributed to this report.

title: Millions are without power as Cuba is hit by latest major blackout
description: [EPA/Shutterstock]...
fullText:
Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.

The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.

Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.

UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.

Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.

Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.

Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.

"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.

"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."

"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."

Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".

The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.

US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

title: Lingering feuds threaten Democrats' bid to reclaim Congress
description:
By Nolan D. McCaskill 
   WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Democrats are seeking to reclaim Congress, but lingering divisions from a bruising run-up to the November election threaten to imperil the party's attempt to claw back power from President Donald Trump's Republicans. 
   With control of both chambers at stake, Democrats have sought to move past the bad blood of the primaries, but in several competitive states, influential party figures have withheld endorsements or so far declined to campaign with nominees for the November 3 US midterm elections. 
   In ‌Maine, the governor has yet to endorse the Democratic US Senate candidate. In Texas, a congresswoman has declined to campaign alongside the state representative who defeated her in the Democratic Senate primary.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Democrats are seeking to reclaim Congress, but lingering divisions from a bruising run-up to the November election threaten to imperil the party's attempt to claw back power from President Donald Trump's Republicans.

With control of both chambers at stake, Democrats have sought to move past the bad blood of the primaries, but in several competitive states, influential party figures have withheld endorsements or so far declined to campaign with nominees for the November 3 US midterm elections.

In ‌Maine, the governor has yet to endorse the Democratic US Senate candidate. In Texas, a congresswoman has declined to campaign alongside the state representative who defeated her in the Democratic Senate primary. In Michigan, establishment centrists are steering clear of the party's progressive Senate ‌pick. In New York, victorious democratic socialists are criticizing congressional Democrats for joining Republicans in condemning socialism. In Florida, the party has yet to rally behind its Senate nominee.

"Whether you are a progressive or an establishment Democrat or a conservative Democrat, we all have a vested interest in getting every single person over the finish line in November," said US Representative ​Summer Lee, a progressive Pennsylvania Democrat up for reelection.

If Democrats fail to unify and win at least one chamber, she warned, "all of our work after that is going to be harder."

Democrats' best path to a Senate majority requires defeating Susan Collins in Maine. Collins is widely considered the most vulnerable Republican senator in the country. But former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, is running without the endorsement of Governor Janet Mills, a onetime Senate candidate who hoped to unseat Collins herself. Mills' office did not respond to a request for comment.

"I would say they're mostly unified," Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, said of Maine Democrats. "The one piece of it that stands out is that Janet Mills has not endorsed Troy Jackson."

Contacted by Reuters, the Maine Democratic Party did not directly address Mills' role but cited turnout for its nominating process and energy on the ground as evidence of unity. "Maine Democrats ‌are united and focused on winning in November," said Devon Murphy-Anderson, the state party's executive director. "Troy has ⁠spent his career fighting for working Mainers and there is real energy behind his campaign to defeat Susan Collins."

In Texas, US Representative Jasmine Crockett has pledged her support to state Representative James Talarico, who defeated her in the Senate primary and is taking on Republican Ken Paxton. But Crockett has repeatedly rejected Talarico's overtures for the two to campaign together, even declining to introduce him at Texas Democrats' state convention in June.

Crockett drew criticism from ⁠social media users last week for appearing on stage in Texas with R&B singer Chris Brown, but not with Talarico, who could become the first Democrat in decades to win a statewide race in Texas. In 2009, Brown pleaded guilty to assaulting then-girlfriend Rihanna and has said domestic violence classes helped him learn from his mistakes.

Crockett has instead said she will focus on lower-profile races, arguing that will also benefit Talarico's Senate campaign.

"As the Democratic nominee, I trust that he has a plan," Crockett told CBS News this month. "I know that their plan wasn't necessarily to include his opponent."

In Michigan, lingering divisions have centered on Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, ​a ​progressive who narrowly leads Republican Mike Rogers in polling in one of the party's must-win states. Some Democrats have expressed discomfort with El-Sayed's association with controversial streamer Hasan ​Piker and with his rhetoric on Israel and Jews, and multiple prominent party figures have yet to endorse him.

After ‌their closely contested Senate primary, US Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan offered her "full support" to El-Sayed, and the two hugged at a unity breakfast the following day. An El-Sayed campaign adviser told Reuters the two camps are in regular communication and that the campaign sees Stevens "as a critical member of the coalition that will beat Mike Rogers."

But it's unclear whether Stevens will campaign with El-Sayed, and others in the party have been openly critical.

US Representative Hillary Scholten and state Senator Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for a congressional seat, have not endorsed El-Sayed. Neither of their campaigns immediately responded to a request for comment.

Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution – a group that works to elect progressive candidates – said there's a double-standard when progressives win against establishment candidates.

"The establishment expects progressives to fall in line when they prevail at the ballot box, but when progressives win, there are some signs of unity, but the entire establishment doesn't really fall in lockstep behind our candidates," he said. "I think that hurts our ability to do job No. 1, which is to beat the Republicans in November."

Others see the tensions differently.

"When you run a campaign that completely shits on the establishment and then you win that campaign ... ‌then you turn around and say, 'I need this machine in order to win,' it is a little bit disingenuous," Democratic consultant Rodell Mollineau said.

TARGETING DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS 'LIKE ME'

The divisions surfaced ​on Capitol Hill earlier this month when eight moderate Democrats joined Republicans in approving a resolution condemning socialism, drawing criticism from New York democratic socialists Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire ​Valdez, who are poised to win US House seats in November after defeating establishment-backed rivals in their primaries.

"This resolution was aimed squarely at ​democratic socialists like me," Chevalier said in a statement. "We don't need a tent that shrinks from its own history. We need a unified party that takes on corporate power, gets money out of politics and delivers for working people."

In Florida, Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, defeated the better-funded retired Lieutenant Colonel Alex ​Vindman by a double-digit margin in August.

Vindman said he would stand beside her "in ​the fight against" Republican Senator Ashley Moody and has donated $825,000 to help Democratic candidates, including $400,000 to the state party to support Nixon and other Florida Democrats.

But it's less clear whether the party is as supportive of Nixon as Vindman has been.

Derrick Scott, chair of Florida's Escambia County Democratic Party, said the party's "vote blue no matter who" message, shorthand for supporting Democratic candidates, appears to come with an exception now that Nixon is the nominee.

"We still have yet to see Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic Party, come out and unequivocally and ​full-throatedly support Angie Nixon," he said.

A Democratic Party spokesperson said it's inaccurate to say the party hasn't rallied ‌behind Nixon, noting Fried recently joined Nixon and another statewide candidate for a joint press conference. The spokesperson said the party is working closely with Nixon and is frequently in touch with her team.

Chanae Jackson, the Nixon campaign's former organizing director, said ​voters are frustrated with party leaders who underestimated Nixon and Democratic organizations too often seek Black voter turnout without building durable support for Black-led campaigns.

"They want our labor, but they don't want our leadership," she said. "They want us to work like a ​dog while they take credit for it."

title: MS NOW and CNN say their journalists were denied access to White House grounds
description:
— Two major news networks were denied access to the White House on Saturday morning, with reporters from CNN and MS NOW both going live to report they'd been barred following a ban imposed by President Donald Trump.
The actions escalated Trump’s long-running efforts to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and is the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump said Friday he would ban both organizations and also Politico, because of their coverage — which he called “fake news.”
CNN issued a statement saying it stood behind its reporters. “We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account,” it said.
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — Two major news networks were denied access to the White House on Saturday morning, with reporters from CNN and MS NOW both going live to report they'd been barred following a ban imposed by President Donald Trump.

The actions escalated Trump's long-running efforts to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and is the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump said Friday he would ban both organizations and also Politico, because of their coverage — which he called "fake news."

CNN issued a statement saying it stood behind its reporters. "We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account," it said. The statement was shown on the air before senior White House reporter Betsy Klein began to report on her ban.

MS NOW also said in a statement that it stands behind its journalists.

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network said in a statement Saturday. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."

Both CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein and MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner went on the air to report they'd been banned from entering the White House.

Network correspondents are usually present on the weekends when the president is in Washington or at nearby Camp David. Trump is at the presidential retreat in Maryland this weekend. Politico journalists typically are not at the White House on Saturdays.

Gardner was turned away and her entry badge confiscated, she said. She noted she had walked through two gates successfully, but once she got to where her badge needed to be scanned, an officer told her it was disabled and asked her to hand it over. He said the decision "was above him," she reported. An MS NOW producer was able to get in, but a photographer's badge was also disabled, Gardner said.

Klein, senior White House reporter at CNN, also said her badge had been deactivated.

CNN media analyst Brian Stelter called the move "a direct threat to press freedom in the United States."

"It's so much bigger than CNN," Stelter said. "This is a free speech test in America."

The president wrote on his social media site Friday that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Minutes later, speaking at an event in the Oval Office, Trump was asked to explain his statement.

"Because they're fake news," he said. "You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it's just fake. That's why their ratings are no good. When you look at MS NOW … , it's fake news."

"And when you look at Politico ... the stories they wrote are fake. So there's a lot of news and there may be others to join them, and maybe they can get better," he said. "But our country has to have honest news."

In his second term, Trump and his administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms.

The move follows the president's decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters. The AP said that it would note when appropriate that Trump had ordered it renamed the "Gulf of America."

The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC. His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation involving ABC over renewal of its broadcast licenses.

It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen.

fullText:
A column of black smoke has been seen near Riyadh's international airport hours after air raid alerts were issued in the Saudi capital.

It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen.

A number of apparent explosions were heard in the capital and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations earlier in the day.

One report suggested a fuel tank had been set on fire near the airport. There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.

An AFP news agency journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to state oil and gas company Aramco.

The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.

Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

On Friday, the Houthis announced that they had thwarted Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sanaa which they said bore the hallmarks of an Islamic State operation.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said Saudi Arabia had carried out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.

He warned the reported attacks on Sanaa would "not go unanswered".

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.

The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.

On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796.

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.

The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.

Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

title: Denmark and Greenland push back on Trump's 'permanent control' claim
description:
, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little 
   COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's ‌security, leaving its precise scope unclear. 
   The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for ‌the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island. 
   Key details of the agreement have not been made public, ​including the degree of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington. 
   Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland. 
   "Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said ‌in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.
fullText:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's ‌security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for ‌the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, ​including the degree of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.

"Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said ‌in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

"A time ⁠of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he said.

Denmark and Greenland ⁠have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

TRUMP'S VISION FOR GREENLAND DEAL

Trump said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend ​the ​security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control ​over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said, ‌adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably not the end of President Trump's ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.

If Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of ‌replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States," he ​said.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said on Saturday that he was pleased with the proposed deal: "The ​agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and ​the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination," he said in a post on Facebook.

Trump's threats, which ‌peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations ​within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland ​into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

Steffen Nielsen, a 49-year-old sales worker living in Copenhagen, told Reuters: "I think that the US is probably going to get ​what they could have had the whole time, if ‌they just asked nicely."

"I don't like it," Kaj Jorgensen, an 80-year-old pensioner, also living in Copenhagen, said of the news. "I don't wish ​the United States to be present anywhere in the Danish Kingdom. I really don't trust Donald Trump."

title: Fundraiser for Lindsay Clancy holdout juror passes $300,000
description:
A fundraiser for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who favored convicting Lindsay Clancy in her closely watched Massachusetts murder trial, has passed $300,000 on crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo.
The 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of her children—Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan—at the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She pleaded not guilty.
Her defense attorney argued that postpartum psychosis had left her not criminally responsible for their deaths. The 12 jurors deliberated for seven days but failed to reach a unanimous verdict, leading Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.
fullText:
A fundraiser for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who favored convicting Lindsay Clancy in her closely watched Massachusetts murder trial, has passed $300,000 on crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo.

The 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of her children—Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan—at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She pleaded not guilty.

Her defense attorney argued that postpartum psychosis had left her not criminally responsible for their deaths. The 12 jurors deliberated for seven days but failed to reach a unanimous verdict, leading Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.

"I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said in a statement previously provided to Newsweek via his lawyer. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

In a statement on Friday on X, GiveSendGo co-founder Jacob Wells said he had spoken with Desronvil and his attorney Edward Paltzik.

“The Lone Juror is being added to the campaign as the recipient. His identity has been verified,” Wells wrote. “Thank you all for your generosity to this campaign.”

In a written statement on X, Paltzik thanked Wells and the fundraiser’s organizers for ensuring that all proceeds would go directly to his client to help pay for necessities after what he described as “death threats, doxxing and harassment.”

He wrote that “Stand With the Juror” would continue as the official and authorized fundraising page, with further updates to be posted there. Paltzik also thanked Wells for his leadership of the fundraising platform and acknowledged others who helped establish and support the campaign.

As of early Saturday, the fundraiser had raised a little over $330,000 of a stated goal of $350,000.

Newsweek reached out to Clancy’s attorney for comment via email on Saturday.

Desronvil, 48, from Massachusetts was the only juror who favored finding Clancy criminally responsible at her murder trial.

His attorney described him in a statement on social media on Thursday as an “American Hero and Champion of Justice [who] loves the United States of America as the greatest country in the world.”

Paltzik added Desronvil was “presently safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England.”

Newsweek previously reported that court records showed Desronvil faced a criminal charge in 2021 for allegedly assaulting his then-wife to which he pleaded not guilty, and the charges were later dismissed, meaning he was not convicted.

Following the mistrial, the case remains unresolved and the murder charges against her are still pending.

The next confirmed court proceeding is a September 29 status hearing in Plymouth Superior Court before Sullivan. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, has filed a renewed motion asking the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty. He argued that the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence to establish criminal responsibility for the killings beyond a reasonable doubt.

Reddington has also said he intends to argue that another prosecution should be barred on double-jeopardy grounds, challenging whether there was sufficient necessity to declare the mistrial.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Tobias Meyjes, Edward Pearcey and Anthony Murray.

title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
description:
Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China.

 Continue reading...
fullText:
When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China.

“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.

Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.

“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.

The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.

In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.

AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.

As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.

Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.

Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition 

“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.

Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.

“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.

Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)

But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.

Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.

“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.

Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.

Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.

“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”

Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.

“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”

Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.

“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”

Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.

Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.

“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.

The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.

Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.

“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.

Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.

“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.

Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.

Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.

Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.

“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”

While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.

As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.

“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.

China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.

“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”

While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.

“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.

Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.

“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

title: ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners
description:
Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group
At the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, in Devon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers.
A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.”
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group

At the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, in Devon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers.

A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.”

Posted to social media after the incident on 28 August, the footage rapidly attracted attention. To some, it was an act of straightforward vandalism; a woman in her 60s and man in his 70s were later arrested and bailed on suspicion of criminal damage and causing danger to road users.

Others, however, believed the woman should be lauded. “Not all heroes wear capes,” reads one Facebook comment on a supporter’s page. “Bideford and Barnstaple next, please,” reads another.

Most people view traffic lights as helpful landmarks that keep road and pavement users safe. To a group who call themselves “Blade Runners”, however, the traffic scanners installed above them increasingly conceal a sinister purpose: to install “phased array electronic assault weapons” on city streets that they claim can carry out mass surveillance and even cause cancer, dementia and sudden death.

Previous activists claiming affiliation to the movement have targeted Ulez cameras in London, resentful at their surveillance and the resulting emission zone charges; there have also been sporadic attacks on 5G mobile network towers, inspired by conspiracy theories that include the suggestion they spread Covid.

Ilfracombe is not the only town where traffic scanners have been attacked. In May, police in Cambridge appealed for information about a suspect after nearly 200 traffic detector units were damaged. In the same month in Sleaford, Lincolnshire, 10 units were vandalised in a week, with the council describing the conspiracy claims as “ridiculous”. In County Durham, a pensioner is facing trial after allegedly damaging units on eight sets of traffic lights.

To Susan Grant-Muller, a professor of technologies and informatics at the University of Leeds’s Institute for Transport Studies, hostility to traffic scanners is puzzling because “this technology, in its most basic form, has been around since the late 70s”. Activists targeting traffic lights do not generally damage the familiar green, amber and red stop-go systems, but instead target additional sensors installed on top that monitor vehicle volume and, in some cases, pedestrian numbers, to allow lights to be phased to help traffic flow smoothly.

“The cameras aren’t recording any personal information at all,” says Grant-Muller. “They aren’t recording faces or any details about the car. They just detect that there is something there, a car or person, and the length of the queue that people are waiting in.”

They are generally only installed at junctions with a history of traffic flow problems, she says – often at the request of concerned local residents – and are welcomed by Living Streets, which promotes pedestrian safety. “Better monitoring technology improves pedestrian safety at traffic lights and crossings, [particularly] when enforcement technology is used as part of a wider approach to road safety,” says Tanya Braun, the charity’s director of external affairs.

None of this convinces those who see a more nefarious purpose behind them. Conspiracies about these scanners fits into a broader fear of surveillance and limits to individual freedom. This is part of a “super-conspiracy” that believers call “the great reset”, says Clare Birchall, a professor of contemporary culture at King’s College London, who has written extensively on technology and conspiracist thinking.

“These super-conspiracies draw all sorts of different things together to give some kind of shape to a whole bunch of different anxieties and fears,” says Birchall. “We’re all worried about technological overreach. Lots of people are worried about datacentres. And I often read conspiracy theories as a vernacular form of critique. It’s an everyday version of what we’re all trying to grasp.

“I’m not surprised at all that [some] people need to find a narrative to find their way through it, because we’re so disenfranchised when it comes to the collection of our data or what happens to that.”

Conspiracies often form in response to frightening events, agrees Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor and chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, “and if you can assign that to a bunch of evil-doers who are responsible, that can provide psychological comfort for certain people, because they’d rather have bad people do bad things, then realise that the world contains effectively random events that you can’t control”.
